To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the accumulation and transfer along a metal pollution gradients of essential and non-essential metals are different and that the transfer of essential metals is more limited than non-essential metals.
the metal transfer along a food chain is dependent on the metal considered, and that the metal content in food is more related to the metal content in soil than to the metal bioavailability in soil.

(i) metal exposure increased with increasing distance from the source of metal pollution; (ii) non-essential elements showed a higher transfer through the food chain; and (iii) the total soil metal content was a better predictor of metal transfer through the food web than the available metal fractions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of metal transfer along a soil-diet food chain.
the transfer and accumulation of metals along a soil-diet-mammal food chain in a natural environment.
a better understanding of metal bioaccumulation and transfer in terrestrial food chains, and the factors that influence this process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
metal exposure of the wood mice was related to the metal content in soil, which is the ultimate source of the metals in the food chain.
metal transfer in a food chain depends on the metal considered, and that the transfer of non- essential metals is more important than the transfer of essential ones.
metal exposure and transfer in the food chain is a complex process, depending on the metal and the compartments involved.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the metal transfer and bioaccumulation in the soil-diet-rodent food chain are mainly determined by the metal content in soil, but the metal bioavailability in soil is also important.

the metal exposure gradient in the soil-diet-plant food chain is mainly driven by the soil metal concentration, while the metal accumulation gradient in the diet-wood mouse compartment is driven by both soil and diet metal concentrations.

the non-essential element transfer is mainly controlled by the metal exposure in soil, while essential element transfer is mainly determined by the metal exposure of the diet and the metal requirements of the organism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of total metal content of soil as a predictor of the metal content of food is not appropriate, and that the use of available metal content of soil should be preferred.
metal transfer and accumulation in a soil-dier-wood mouse foodchain are not only dependent on metal bioavailability in soil, but are also strongly influenced by the chemical form of the metal.
the metal exposure of the wood mouse is mainly driven by the diet and not the soil.
